question: Are these groups that having lost Aleppo might align with the so-called Islamic State elsewhere in Syria, or are they distinct and different and opposed to that group?
true_answer_verbatim: I think that anyone who considers himself a Syrian nationalist - in essence a Syria-firster - would find it very, very, very difficult to sign up with ISIS because ISIS of course believes it has a worldwide mission. And ISIS really has not been engaged in fighting Bashar al-Assad very much in any event.
true_answer_paraphrased: Anyone who considers himself a Syrian nationalist, meaning a Syria-firster, would find it very difficult to join ISIS because ISIS believes it has a worldwide mission, and ISIS has not been fighting Bashar al-Assad very much anyway.

options.text: Many fighters leaving Homs and Hama share the exact same radical ideology as Daesh, and once they regroup in the eastern desert near Raqqa, commanders like Zahran Alloush will likely merge their brigades directly into the Islamic State.
options.why: Answer 1 argues that Syrian nationalists would find it difficult to join ISIS due to differing ideologies and goals, whereas Answer 2 argues that many departing fighters share ISIS's radical ideology and will likely merge their brigades into the Islamic State.
